corrected_value.authors: Rácz, P., Hay, J., & Pierrehumbert, J. B.
corrected_value.title: Social salience discriminates learnability of contextual cues in an artificial language.

decisions.quote:
In this study, we investigated the learning of indexical features by English-speaking adults using a novel experimental paradigm. In a conceptual replication of Rácz, Hay, and Pierrehumbert (2017), participants learned an allomorphy pattern cued by a given social context. The social contexts were represented by conversation partners who differed by age, ethnicity, and/or gender and were positioned in various ways. The results showed that, after training, the participants were able to learn that different types of conversation partners prefer different types of allomorphs but that learning and generalization hinged on the social relevance of the cue represented by the conversation partner. These results suggest that the relevance of cues in an individual's past social experience influences their storage and learnability even at very early stages of learning a word pattern.

decisions.reason: In the complete published article text and expanded references, both shipped row 772 and fresh blind coding (target 0) accurately identify Rácz, Hay, and Pierrehumbert (2017), 'Social salience discriminates learnability of contextual cues in an artificial language' (Frontiers in Psychology, 8, 51; DOI: 10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00051). The Abstract, Introduction, The Current Study, Method, and Discussion explicitly identify Rácz et al. (2017) as the empirical study being conceptually replicated and extended. Other cited works (such as Foulkes, 2010; Docherty et al., 2013; Samara et al., 2017; Needle & Pierrehumbert, 2018) are discussed as theoretical motivation or convergent background literature rather than targets re-tested by this experiment.

decisions.quote:
The two categories in between were eminently learnable but generalization to new conversation partners was not straightforward—participants benefited from familiarity. This challenges the interpretation that we alluded to above, namely, that participants either learned the context-pattern association or not. This seems to be true for the gender cue, but not for age and ethnicity.

In summary, a larger proportion of participants was successful at learning meaningful contextual associations (gender, age, ethnicity) than a nonmeaningful association (view). Gender, in particular, was the easiest for participants to learn out of the three associations. Gender-based associations were generalized straightforwardly to new conversation partners, but those based on age and ethnicity were also generalized, but to a lesser degree. This indicated that a robustly learnable distinction was also robust to generalization.

Secondary Models to Test the Robustness of Evidence for Learning Meaningful Contextual Associations
decisions.reason: Rácz et al. (2017) reported that a socially salient cue (gender) was learned and generalized much more easily than a nonsocial spatial-orientation cue (view). Although Data Analysis notes that the two original diminutive cells—gender(view) (n=47) and view(gender) (n=48)—are reused and pooled with 10 new conditions (n=340) so Model 1's pooled gender-versus-view estimate (est=0.79, 95% CI [0.19, 1.39]) is not an isolated rerun of those two cells, the new conditions conceptually re-test the original social-salience claim across new operationalizations: gender(age), gender(ethnicity) (diminutive and plural), view(age), and the entirely new age and ethnicity conditions. In Model 1, the new age main-cue conditions show higher accuracy than view (est=0.79, 95% CI [0.21, 1.38]) with partner-familiarity mediation (est=0.16, 95% CI [0.03, 0.29]), and the new ethnicity conditions show learning and partial generalization (partner-familiarity interaction est=0.25, 95% CI [0.09, 0.41]). Across all gender and view conditions (including new gender(age), gender(ethnicity), and view(age) extensions), partner familiarity showed no interaction in Model 1 or in 0/100 resampled runs (Model 4), reflecting ceiling generalization for gender versus chance guessing for view; Model 2 (fit solely on the four new ethnicity/gender diminutive and plural conditions) shows pattern invariance (p=.94). Under the codebook, the authors' explicit conclusion confirming that socially salient cues are learned and generalized better than the irrelevant view cue establishes a successful outcome.

decisions.quote:
The task layout might have had an effect on the results. The task was entirely visual and responses were in a forced-choice format. An open format would likely have resulted in a different pattern of responses, but it would have also required the participants to effectively memorize the entire syllabary, rendering an already challenging task even more difficult.

With this in mind, we return to our starting hypotheses: The results presented here indicate that a socially salient cue is more learnable than an irrelevant cue and that certain salient cues are easier to learn than others. In addition, the salience of a cue plays into the extent to which the cue can be generalized (from familiar conversation partners to new ones). These results have expanded on our Rácz et al. (2017) study that showed that it is possible to study contextual language learning using artificial language methods. We expanded on this study by broadening the range of contexts that we investigated and found that their real-life prevalence manifests in how participants learn and generalize them.
decisions.reason: While Data Analysis explicitly states that observations from the two Rácz et al. (2017) conditions—gender(view) (n=47) and view(gender) (n=48)—were reused and analyzed in combination with the new conditions, the study is not merely a re-analysis (reproduction) of the 2017 dataset. As shown in Method and Table 2, the authors collected new experimental data from 340 additional participants across 10 new cue/pattern conditions—gender(age), gender(ethnicity) diminutive and plural, view(age), age(ethnicity), age(gender), age(view), ethnicity(age), and ethnicity(gender) diminutive and plural—extending both the training contrasts and test-phase conversation partner generalizations. Under the codebook, collecting new data in additional participant samples to conceptually re-test the previously published finding that social salience governs cue learnability and generalization in an artificial language is a replication.
